title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Priya Nair
content:
Overview:

This document codifies Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture standards and canonical ADRs for API design, coding style, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It is intended to be the single, opinionated reference for engineers and architects when designing or changing services that interact with the inference platform.

Scope:
- Public and internal REST/gRPC APIs and SDKs
- Service coding standards and repository layout
- Cloud and on-prem infra patterns, networking and capacity planning
- Model serving contracts, versioning, and fallback policies
- Observability (metrics, traces, logs) and alerting requirements
- Performance SLOs and benchmarking expectations
- Decision records for major architectural choices (ADRs)

Principles (summary):
1. Developer ergonomics first: APIs should be intuitive and consistent across surface area (hosted, dedicated, private).
2. Production-first: every service must ship with SLOs, runbooks, and CI checks that prevent regressions.
3. Explicit compatibility: model and API compatibility guarantees must be versioned and discoverable.
4. Cost-awareness: defaults should favor predictable economics (limits, batching, caching).
5. Observability-as-code: dashboards and alerts are part of PRs that change runtime behavior.

1) API Standards
- External API (customer-facing): REST/HTTP with JSON over TLS for general purpose requests; HTTP/2 + gRPC for streaming and binary payloads (embeddings, large-batch operations).
- Internal service-to-service: gRPC with protobufs for high-throughput links (router -> runtime, runtime -> backend cache). REST only if human-facing or integrates with third-party webhooks.
- Versioning: semantic versioning for public endpoints. Path-based versioning for major versions: /v1/, /v2/. Deprecation policy: min 90 days for public breaking changes + migration guides.
- Authentication and authz: All APIs require bearer tokens (JWT or internally-issued opaque tokens). Customer data plane endpoints must support mutual TLS when in private deployments.
- Errors and retries: Use HTTP status semantics. Provide structured error body with fields: code, message, retriable (bool), details. Retries should be idempotency-aware and bounded by a standard backoff policy (max 3 attempts, jittered exponential backoff starting at 100ms).
- Pagination and streaming: Cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. Streaming endpoints must support resume semantics and server-side heartbeats.

Example API contract (text):
POST /v1/generate
Request: {
  "model": "redwood-v1-alpha",
  "input": "string",
  "max_tokens": 128,
  "stream": false
}
Response: {
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "model_version": "2026-02-15",
  "output": "string",
  "latency_ms": 123
}

2) Coding & Repo Standards
- Language choices: primary services in Go (control plane, routing), Python for evaluation/eval-harness and model onboarding helpers, Rust/C++ only for performance-critical runtime kernels.
- Linters & formatters: every repo must include a pre-commit config and CI check that runs formatting (gofmt/black), linters (golangci-lint, flake8), and static checks.
- Module boundaries: dependencies must be explicit; core infra libs live under /libs and are versioned independently. No heavy ML dependencies in control-plane services.
- API clients/SDKs: generate from OpenAPI/protobufs. SDKs must include small, idiomatic examples and a quickstart README.
- Tests: Unit tests for logic, integration tests for infra interactions, and an e2e smoke test that runs in CI against a staging cluster. Coverage gate: maintain > 60% for new services; critical services target > 80%.
- PR expectations: each PR should include a short design summary, a list of modified SLOs (if any), and an owner for rollouts.

3) Infra Standards
- IaC: Terraform for cloud provisioning, Helm/Kustomize for Kubernetes manifests. Stateful infra must document backup and restore steps in the repo.
- Network: follow zero-trust principles; services authenticate with short-lived identities (workload identity, SPIFFE where available). VPC peering and private connectivity are standard for Redwood Private customers.
- GPU fleet: capacity planning must include GPU type (A100/H100), utilization targets (avg 60% over 24h), and overcommit policies. Autoscaling thresholds are in the GPU Fleet doc (link in related_pages).
- Secrets & keys: use a centralized KMS integrated with customer key options for Private. No plaintext secrets in repos.
- CI/CD: automated canary deploys for control-plane changes. Major runtime/kernel updates require a staged rollout: dev -> staging (perf regression gate) -> canary on 5% -> gradual ramp to 100%.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model manifests: every model must include a manifest file with these fields: model_id, architecture, quantization_profile, tokenization, max_context, memory_estimate, compatible_kernels, and quality_baseline_id. (see Model Onboarding doc)
- Versioning: immutable model artifacts; deploy with a semantic model-version tag and a human-readable release notes entry.
- Fallback policies: router config must specify fallback chain (primary variant -> quantized variant -> smaller contextual model) with clear latency and quality tradeoffs.
- KV cache and prefix caching: services must expose cache hit metrics and provide configuration knobs for TTL and size per-model. Defaults: prefix cache TTL 24h for public models; customer-managed per-deployment TTL optional.
- Quantization & profiles: maintain a set of tested quantization profiles (int8, int4, fp16) with expected quality regressions documented in the quantization_profiles library. Use A/B evaluation before rolling a quantized profile to production.

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics: all services must export Prometheus metrics. Standard metric names must follow the namespace: redwood_<service>_<metric>_total/gauge/histogram. Examples: redwood_inference_tokens_generated_total, redwood_router_requests_in_flight_gauge.
- Traces: instrument key RPC boundaries and model runtime calls with OpenTelemetry. Trace sampling: default 1% for high-traffic routes, 100% for debug canaries.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with these fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, tenant_id (if available), message, details.
- Dashboards & runbooks: every service must include a dashboards manifest and an associated runbook that explains common alerts, triage steps, and escalation contacts. Dashboards are code-reviewed and shipped with the feature PR.
- Alerting: follow SLO-driven alerts (see SLOs below). Critical alerts (P0) should page on-call; P1 (degradation) send to Slack #sre-alerts and update status page if customer impact is expected.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs
- Platform-level SLOs (example targets):
  - Hosted API availability: 99.95% monthly (excludes scheduled maintenance)
  - Request latency (text-gen, small model): p95 < 120ms, p99 < 350ms for 1-32 token generations on hosted regions
  - Embedding latency (single): p95 < 50ms, p99 < 150ms
  - Throughput: batch path throughput measured per-GPU, documented in the benchmarking suite
- Error budget & paging: SRE maintains an error budget; if monthly availability falls below target, the product/eng incident playbook runs and new feature releases may be paused.
- Benchmarks: the runtime team maintains a benchmarking-and-perf-suite that outputs standardized reports for each model/hardware combination. Benchmarks must include: cold-start time, per-token latency, KV-cache hit impact, and memory footprint.

Sample performance table (example):
| Model Variant | Hardware | p95 latency (ms) | p99 latency (ms) | tokens/s (single GPU) | notes |
|---------------|----------|------------------|------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| redwood-v1-small | A100 | 95 | 280 | 1200 | baseline fp16
| redwood-v1-quant-int8 | A100 | 110 | 340 | 1350 | ~3% quality loss vs fp16

7) ADRS (Decision Records)
We record major architecture decisions below. Full ADRs are terse but include motivation, alternatives, decision, consequences, and migration plan.

ADR-2025-09: Standardize internal RPCs on gRPC + protobuf\- Status: accepted\- Decision: Use gRPC for internal high-throughput RPCs and streaming; REST for external/customer-facing and webhooks.\- Rationale: gRPC enables lower CPU overhead, better streaming semantics, and strongly-typed contracts for our high-throughput routing paths.\- Alternatives considered: stay REST-only (rejected: higher serialization costs); use Thrift (rejected: smaller ecosystem).\- Consequences: add protobuf generation into CI; SDK generation step added to control plane build. Migration plan: Gradual adapter layer for legacy REST endpoints; 6-month migration window.

ADR-2026-01: Default to prefix KV cache + request-level batching\- Status: accepted\- Decision: Router will enable prefix KV cache by default and use workload-aware batching (continuous batching where sensible).\- Rationale: Measured 28% token-cost reduction on typical customer workloads in staging.\- Alternatives: On-demand caching only (rejected: higher request latency and cost).\- Consequences: Must add cache metrics and tenant isolation controls; update privacy/security docs for cache scope. Rollout: Canary on 10% of traffic for 2 weeks with quality regressions monitored.

ADR-2026-02: Quantized model fallback chain as first-class policy\- Status: in_review\- Decision: Make quantized variants (int8/int4) first-class model variants in the model catalog and expose routing policies to prefer non-quantized models only when quality gates fail.\- Rationale: Enables lower cost without disrupting customer apps while preserving an upgrade path.\- Migration: Model owners must provide quality evaluation reports and a compatibility baseline before a quantized variant can be added to the catalog.

8) Change & Rollout Procedures
1. Design PR: Describe change, impacted services, new metrics and SLO adjustments, and ADR if the change modifies architecture.
2. Review: At least one reviewer from runtime, SRE, and product (if customer-facing impact).
3. Staging tests: Run perf benchmarks and smoke e2e tests; collect traces.
4. Canary rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated gates (latency, error rate, quality eval).
5. Postmortem: If any gate is breached, abort rollout and open incident review; update ADRs/runbooks as necessary.

9) Compliance & Security Notes
- Data residency: Private deployments must document data flow and storage locations in the customer requirements library.
- Audit logging: All model-serving requests must emit an audit event for billing-eligible customers (subject to sampling policy).
- RBAC: Administrative routes require fine-grained RBAC and MFA for control-plane role changes.

10) Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- Generate proto clients (Go):
  protoc --go_out=plugins=grpc:./gen -I protos protos/router.proto
- Run local perf harness:
  ./scripts/run_benchmark.sh --model redwood-v1-small --gpu a100 --batch-size 16

11) Ownership & Maintenance
- Document owner: Priya Nair (architecture-and-standards lead)
- Runtime & infra owners: eng-serving-runtime team
- Review cadence: Annual review or earlier on major infra changes.

If you change standards described here, add or update an ADR and include tests/dashboards as part of the PR.
